title: Of repentance
hookLine: he distrusts dramatic repentance and prefers steady change (Essays 3.2)

cards: New Year's Day. The gym is packed, the fridge is full of vegetables, and a list on the counter says this year everything changes. By February the list is under a takeout menu.
Big turning points feel wonderful; they don't always last. Montaigne noticed something like this in himself, in the same essay as yesterday's sentence, the one called Of repentance.
And his confession sounds odd under that title. He says he rarely repents.

teach.h: A HABIT ISN'T UNDONE BY A SIGH.
teach.b: First, what he means. Montaigne isn't bragging that he never does wrong; he has listed his own faults plainly elsewhere. He's talking about the regret that flares up, weeps, and changes nothing.
A fault that has become a habit, he says, isn't undone by a sigh. Real regret would show in how he lives tomorrow, not in how loudly he feels it today.

Second, the pattern within. A person needs a pattern inside, he says, a standard of their own to test their actions against. Not the crowd's applause, not a show of sorrow: a quiet inner measure that is there every day.
Steady change starts there. Third, the regret of old age. When the appetites fade with age, he says, people sometimes call that repentance.
He calls it weakness, not wisdom: the vice left, but the person didn't choose to change.
He'd rather be good on purpose than good because he's tired. Fourth, a word about faith.
Montaigne isn't arguing against anyone's practice of confession or turning back to God; he's describing his own temperament and what he trusts in himself.
For him, change worth the name is slow, ordinary, and visible in habits: one small thing done differently, again and again, without a speech.

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of repentance often take from it a preference for slow, lasting changes in habit over dramatic resolutions that fade.

games.q: you've caught yourself in an old bad habit again. what would Montaigne trust?
o: a tearful vow to change everything.
a small change, kept up in tomorrow's habits.
waiting until age makes the habit fade.
games.why: a habit, he says, isn't undone by a sigh, and fading with age isn't virtue. change worth the name shows in how you live.

practice: Think of one habit you'd like to shift, and make it small enough to do today, tomorrow and the day after: a glass of water before coffee, a kind word before a hard one, a little earlier to bed. No vow, no list on the counter.
Just picture yourself doing it once, plainly.
